newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish cash pool plan gets mixed reaction.
newsitem.headline: Turkish cash pool plan gets mixed reaction.

text.p: Turkish bureaucrats, economists and businessmen gave contrasting reactions on Friday to a government plan to pool public revenues to help poor state institutions and better control state funds.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan said on Tuesday a central cash management system would be set up to enable state companies which need money to tap revenues made by profit-making state institutions and firms.
Gazi Ercel, governor of the central bank, said the plan would enable the government to control money from one centre.
"The system will make it possible to monitor public accounts simultaneously and from one centre," he told a meeting. "Movements of state funds will easily be controlled," he said.
But economist Erhan Isil said the plan, prepared by four state banks, would contravene the rules of free market economic policy Turkey adopted in the 1980s.

"Taking the monetary management of the state economic enterprises, which are commercial and industrial institutions, into the central state is diametrically opposed to the concept of market economy," he wrote in the economic daily Dunya.
He said the government plan, yet to be approved after cabinet debates, did not clarify whether non-profit state institutions would be included in the system.
"The government had better prepare a management system for the cash flow of its institutions, which fluctuates according to seasons," he said.

The plan will not allow money making state companies like petrochemicals producer Petkim and petroleum marketer Petrol Ofisi to invest their profits or excess cash in financial instruments, mainly in repurchase agreements, or repo.

Repo, the trading of t-bills with maturities from overnight up to 32 days, is an attractive short-term financial tool for small- and large-size investors who do not have to pay income tax for their returns.
Erbakan said the system would reduce the treasury's borrowing requirement. The treasury borrows mainly to close the deficits of government institutions and companies.
Electricity producer TEAS and distributor TEDAS, postal services PTT, oil refiner Tupras and coal producer TKI are among biggest loss-making state companies whose losses amount to trillions of lira.
Under the plan, part of the government's two revenue-raising packages, a state company which needs cash can draw money from the common pool instead of resorting to the treasury's borrowed funds.
Erbakan said the plan would not disrupt the implementation of the individual budgets of each government company.

But the Ankara Industrialists and Businessmen's Association (ASIAD) said the plan would create problems when budgets were prepared by parliament with varying priorities for each government institution.
"Prorities may clash during the preparation of the budgets of key institutions in the defence, agriculture and other sectors," it said in a statement.
